why: Corrects live posts that promise things a generated site cannot do, and cannot be made to do by any prompt. The permanent facts: there is no server, database or mail path behind a published site, so a form on one delivers nothing (lib/foundation.ts ships react and react-dom only; there is no generated backend anywhere); it is ONE page — lib/agent.ts SYSTEM, 'Multi-page: this is a single-page app' — a rule that is already deployed; and app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts serves every site under default-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; connect-src 'none', which rules out uploaded photography, remote galleries and map embeds. NOTE ON WORDING: the working tree's lib/agent.ts adds two rules — never invent facts about a real business, and never build a control that only pretends to work — that HEAD does not have, so they are not deployed yet. Every replacement below is deliberately written to be true both before and after that ships: it states what a form on the site does (nothing), never what the builder currently agrees to draw. These are the highest-severity errors of the three groups — a reader acts on them by pointing real patients at a form that throws their appointment away.
detect: collects the request and sends it to you

edits.find: A simple form where a patient enters their name, contact info, preferred day/time, and reason for the visit. Kodely can build you a genuinely good-looking, professional appointment-request page and contact form. To be clear about what that means today: it collects the request and sends it to you — it does not yet sync automatically to a calendar or scheduling system. Most small practices are fine with this as a starting point: the request comes in, your front desk confirms by phone or email, same as an inquiry from any other channel.
edits.replace: One obvious, impossible-to-miss way to get in touch. Be precise about what that is, because it is the one thing on this page you must not get wrong: a Kodely site is front-end only. There is no server behind it, no database, and no mail path — so a form on it has nowhere to send anything, and an appointment typed into one is gone. What works with no server is a large tap-to-call tel: button, an email link, and a prominent "Book online" button pointing at whatever scheduling system you already use. Ask for those.
edits.note: The old text said the form 'collects the request and sends it to you'. Nothing receives it: a generated site has no server and no mail path.

edits.find: Kodely can build a professional, well-designed appointment-request page and contact form. It collects the patient's request — it doesn't yet connect to a real calendar or scheduling backend automatically, so your team confirms the appointment manually, the same way you'd handle a phone or email inquiry.
edits.replace: No — and you should not put a booking form on the site either. There is no backend behind a generated site, so a form has nothing to submit to and every request typed into one is silently discarded. Use the parts that work with no server: a tap-to-call number, an email link, and a button pointing at the booking system you already use.

edits.find: A clear, prominent way to request an appointment — name, phone, preferred day, and what's bothering them. Worth being upfront here: a Kodely-built site gives you a genuinely good-looking, working request form and a clear "Call Us" path, but it doesn't connect to a calendar or booking database on its own yet. You'll want to point the form's contact info at whatever scheduling tool or front-desk process you already use, or simply have staff follow up on submissions.
edits.replace: A clear, prominent way to get in touch. Worth being upfront here: a Kodely-built site has no server behind it, so a request form on it would have nowhere to send a request — a form that silently discards an enquiry is worse for your patients than no form at all. What you want instead is a "Call us" button wired to a tel: link, an email link, and a "Book online" button pointing at whatever scheduling tool you already use.
edits.note: 'Working request form' and 'follow up on submissions' both imply submissions exist. They do not.

Point people at your existing scheduling tool with a link-out button, or at your phone with a tap-to-call link; both work from the moment you publish.

edits.find: • What you don't get yet: a backend. There's no database behind the form, so a submitted appointment request doesn't get saved anywhere and no email or SMS notification goes out. The form is real UI — real inputs, real client-side behavior — but submissions aren't persisted or delivered yet. Wiring a form to actually save appointments and notify the business is coming in a future release, and it's the natural next step once you've got the front end looking right.

A booking form on a generated site is a dead end: no database stores the request, no email or SMS goes out, and the person who filled it in has no way of knowing that.
